intro: Nine modules follow the RHCSA (EX200) objectives for RHEL 10. Each has a study guide, exam tips, key terms, visual slides, and a narrated lesson. RHCSA is fully hands-on, so work through the Labs tab and practice on a RHEL 10 virtual machine (Red Hat's no-cost Developer Subscription lets you install one).

sources.title: Red Hat: EX200 Red Hat Certified System Administrator exam (objectives)
RHCSA v10 (EX200) training playlist – Nehra Classes (YouTube)
sources.note: Free · RHCSA on RHEL 10 · 103 videos · checked October 2026

modules.title: Understand and use essential tools
modules.summary: Work fluently at the shell: redirection, grep and regular expressions, SSH and su, tar archives, text editing, file management, links, standard permissions, and finding help in local documentation.

guide.html: Essential tools underpin every other task. On the exam you'll save filtered output to files, find files by owner and copy them, build archives, create links, and set permissions, often as small standalone tasks.

grep with regular expressions (^, $, ., *, [ ]; -E for + ? | {n}), -i, -v, -r, -n. Save output with >, append with >>, redirect errors with 2> or both with &>. Pipe through sort, uniq, wc, head, tail. find / -user harry -type f -exec cp -a {} /root/found/ \; finds and copies files; other tests include -name, -size +30M, -perm -4000, -mmin. Read the task carefully: exact output file, order, and whether to keep duplicates.

tar -czf archive.tar.gz dir (gzip), -cjf (bzip2), -cJf (xz); -tf lists; -xf ... -C dir extracts. ln -s target link makes a symlink; ln target link a hard link (same file system, files only). Permissions: chmod 750 or u+x,g-w; chown user:group; special bits with a leading digit (2770 for SGID directories). Remote access: ssh user@host, scp, sftp; switch users with su - user or sudo -i. Editing: know vim (i, Esc, :wq, :q!, /search, :%s/a/b/g) because it's always there.

The exam has no internet, so practice finding answers with man (sections 1, 5, 8), man -k keyword, command --help, info, and /usr/share/doc. Example: man 5 fstab for fstab fields, man semanage-fcontext for the regex example, man nmcli-examples for networking.

tips: Create target directories before find -exec cp.
tar letters: c x t f with z (gzip), j (bzip2), J (xz).
ln -s TARGET LINKNAME (target first).
Use man -k and man nmcli-examples instead of the internet.
Read every task twice: exact paths, names, and formats are graded.
terms: Pattern for matching text in grep, sed, and vim.
Sending output or errors to files with > >> 2>.
Runs a command on each file that matches.
A file pointing to another path.
Another directory entry for the same inode.
New files inherit the directory's group.
Switch user with a full login environment.

slides.title: Essential tools
script: Welcome to the RHCSA essential tools module. These commands come up in nearly every exam task, so they need to be automatic.
Work through each example in a terminal or in the labs.

slides.title: Find and filter
script: grep searches inside files, and find searches the file tree by name, owner, size, or permissions.
A classic task: find every file owned by a user and copy it into a directory, keeping attributes. Use find with dash exec and cp dash a.

slides.title: Archives and links
script: Create compressed archives with tar and the right compression letter, then list them to check the contents.
Symbolic links point to a path and can cross file systems; hard links share an inode and must stay on one file system.

slides.title: Permissions recap
script: Permissions are owner, group, and others with read four, write two, execute one.
Add a leading digit for special bits: 2 for SGID on shared directories, 1 for the sticky bit.

slides.title: Review: essential tools
script: You've finished the essential tools module. RHCSA is fully hands-on, so repeat each task in the labs until you can do it without looking anything up.
Always ask: will this still work after a reboot? Then verify, and take the question set.

modules.title: Create simple shell scripts
modules.summary: Write Bash scripts that use conditionals, loops, script arguments, and command output, with correct exit codes and permissions.

guide.html: You'll be asked to write a short script that meets a precise specification, such as searching for files, processing arguments, or printing results, saved at a given path and executable.

Start with #!/bin/bash, save it at the exact path requested (often /usr/local/bin/name so it's in PATH), and run chmod +x. Arguments: $1, $2, "$@" (all), $# (count). Exit codes: exit 0 for success, non-zero for errors; $? holds the last status. Capture output with var=$(command).

if [ $# -eq 0 ]; then echo "Usage: $0 dir" >&2; exit 1; fi. File tests: -f, -d, -e, -r, -x; strings =, !=, -z (empty); numbers -eq -ne -lt -le -gt -ge. Loops: for f in /etc/*.conf; do ...; done, for i in {1..5}, while read -r line; do ...; done < file. case "$1" in start) ...;; *) ...;; esac handles options.

Combine scripts with the tools you already know: find, grep, awk '{print $1}', cut, sort -u. Example: for user in $(awk -F: '$3 >= 1000 {print $1}' /etc/passwd); do echo "$user: $(id -Gn $user)"; done. Test your script with different inputs, including none.

tips: Put the script exactly where the task says and chmod +x it.
Quote variables: "$1", "$@".
Use -eq for numbers and = for strings.
Send errors to stderr with >&2 and exit non-zero.
Test with no arguments, one argument, and bad input.
terms: All arguments, each kept as a separate word.
Multi-branch pattern match ending with esac.

slides.title: Shell scripting
script: The RHCSA scripting objective is about small, practical scripts. You'll combine tests, loops, arguments, and the output of other commands.
Keep scripts simple and test them before moving on.

slides.title: Arguments and exit codes
script: Check how many arguments you received with dollar hash, and print a usage message to standard error if it's wrong.
Exit with zero on success and a non-zero code on failure so other commands can tell what happened.

slides.title: Tests and loops
script: Square bracket tests check files, strings, and numbers. Remember the spaces inside the brackets.
For loops walk a list or glob, while read loops walk lines in a file, and case picks a branch by pattern.

slides.title: Using command output
script: Command substitution puts another command's output into a variable or a loop list.
Pipe output into while read to process it line by line, for example reading users from etc passwd with awk.

slides.title: Review: shell scripting
script: You've finished the shell scripting module. RHCSA is fully hands-on, so repeat each task in the labs until you can do it without looking anything up.
Always ask: will this still work after a reboot? Then verify, and take the question set.

modules.title: Operate running systems
modules.summary: Boot, reboot, and shut down; boot into different targets; recover root access; manage processes, priorities, and tuning profiles; use and preserve journals; control services; and transfer files securely.

guide.html: You must control the boot process, interrupt it to regain access, manage processes and services, and make logs persistent.

systemctl get-default / set-default multi-user.target (text) or graphical.target. systemctl isolate switches now. One-time targets at the GRUB menu: press e, append systemd.unit=rescue.target (or emergency.target), press Ctrl+X. Root password reset (RHEL 9/10): add rd.break (or init=/bin/bash), then mount -o remount,rw /sysroot, chroot /sysroot, passwd root, touch /.autorelabel, exit, and let it reboot. Without the relabel, SELinux may block logins.

Find heavy processes with top (P for CPU, M for memory) or ps aux --sort=-%cpu. Stop them with kill, kill -9, pkill, killall. Change priority: nice -n 10 cmd, renice -n 5 -p PID. Tuning: systemctl enable --now tuned, tuned-adm recommend, tuned-adm profile virtual-guest, tuned-adm active.

journalctl with -u unit, -p err, -b, --since, -f. Make the journal persistent: Storage=persistent in /etc/systemd/journald.conf (or mkdir /var/log/journal) and systemctl restart systemd-journald; then journalctl -b -1 shows the previous boot. Services: systemctl enable --now, status, is-enabled. Secure transfers with scp, sftp, rsync -av.

tips: set-default changes boots; isolate changes now.
Root reset: rd.break → remount rw → chroot → passwd → touch /.autorelabel.
Lower nice = higher priority; only root can go below 0.
Make the journal persistent before you need previous-boot logs.
enable --now both starts and enables a service.
terms: systemd group of units representing a system state.
Single-user maintenance target with basic services.
Kernel argument that stops boot inside the initramfs.
Flag file that triggers an SELinux relabel at boot.
Service that applies performance tuning profiles.

slides.title: Operating running systems
script: This module covers controlling a running RHEL system: changing targets, recovering a lost root password, managing processes, tuning, and logs.
The root password reset is a classic exam task, so practice it until it's routine.

slides.title: Resetting the root password
script: At the GRUB menu, edit the entry and add rd dot break to the kernel line. You land in a shell inside the initramfs.
Remount sysroot read-write, chroot into it, set the root password, and touch dot autorelabel so SELinux fixes the shadow file's label at the next boot.

slides.title: Processes and priorities
script: Find the busiest processes with top or ps sorted by CPU or memory.
End runaway processes with kill or pkill, and adjust priority with nice when starting or renice for running processes.

slides.title: Tuning and journals
script: Enable tuned and apply the recommended profile with tuned adm.
Use journalctl filters to find problems, and make the journal persistent so logs from earlier boots are kept.

slides.title: Review: operating running systems
script: You've finished the operating running systems module. RHCSA is fully hands-on, so repeat each task in the labs until you can do it without looking anything up.
Always ask: will this still work after a reboot? Then verify, and take the question set.

modules.title: Configure local storage
modules.summary: Create and delete GPT partitions, build LVM physical volumes, volume groups, and logical volumes, mount by UUID or label, and add partitions, logical volumes, and swap without disturbing existing data.

guide.html: Storage tasks are worth a lot and are easy to get wrong. Expect to create a volume group with a specific extent size, a logical volume of a given size or number of extents, and swap that activates at boot.

Inspect with lsblk and blkid. Create GPT partitions with parted (mklabel gpt, mkpart name xfs 1MiB 1GiB, set 1 lvm on), gdisk, or fdisk. Run partprobe or udevadm settle if the kernel doesn't see the change. Never touch partitions that hold existing data unless told to.

pvcreate /dev/vdb1, vgcreate -s 16M vgdata /dev/vdb1 (extent size), lvcreate -n lvdata -L 1G vgdata or -l 50 (extents) or -l 100%FREE. Grow a VG with vgextend. Inspect with pvs, vgs, lvs, vgdisplay (PE size and free PE). Devices appear at /dev/vgdata/lvdata and /dev/mapper/vgdata-lvdata.

Mount by UUID or LABEL in /etc/fstab so names can't shift. Swap: mkswap /dev/vgdata/lvswap, add UUID=... none swap defaults 0 0, then swapon -a and verify with swapon --show. After editing fstab, run systemctl daemon-reload and mount -a; a broken fstab can stop the system from booting.

tips: -L is size (1G); -l is extents (50) or percentages (100%FREE).
Set the PE size at vgcreate time with -s.
Use UUID= or LABEL= in fstab.
Swap needs mkswap, an fstab entry, and swapon -a.
Test fstab with mount -a before any reboot.
terms: GUID Partition Table, the modern partition scheme.
Disk or partition initialized for LVM.
Pool of storage from one or more PVs.
Usable block device carved from a VG.
Allocation unit of a volume group (default 4 MiB).
Unique identifier of a file system or swap area.
Disk space used as overflow memory.

slides.title: Local storage
script: This module covers building storage: partitions, LVM, and swap, all configured to survive reboots.
Storage tasks are high value, so practice them in the labs until the commands are automatic.

slides.title: Building LVM
script: Initialize physical volumes, combine them into a volume group, and carve logical volumes from it.
If a task asks for a specific extent size, set it with dash s at vgcreate. Size logical volumes in bytes with capital L or in extents with lowercase l.

slides.title: Persistent mounts
script: Look up the UUID with blkid and add a line to fstab: device, mount point, type, options, and two zeros.
Reload systemd, run mount dash a, and check with findmnt before you reboot.

slides.title: Adding swap
script: Create a new partition or logical volume, format it with mkswap, and add it to fstab with mount point none and type swap.
Activate it with swapon dash a and confirm with swapon dash dash show. Existing swap and data must stay untouched.

slides.title: Review: local storage
script: You've finished the local storage module. RHCSA is fully hands-on, so repeat each task in the labs until you can do it without looking anything up.
Always ask: will this still work after a reboot? Then verify, and take the question set.

modules.title: Create and configure file systems
modules.summary: Create, mount, and use VFAT, ext4, and XFS file systems; mount NFS shares and configure autofs; extend logical volumes with their file systems; and diagnose and correct file permission problems.

guide.html: You'll format and mount file systems persistently, connect to NFS (directly and through autofs), grow logical volumes online, and fix permission problems.

mkfs.xfs, mkfs.ext4, mkfs.vfat; set labels with -L (or xfs_admin -L, e2label). Mount points must exist (mkdir -p). Add to /etc/fstab, then mount -a and findmnt. VFAT has no Unix ownership, so use uid=, gid=, umask= options. Use nofail for optional devices.

List exports with showmount -e server. Persistent NFS mount: server:/export /mnt/point nfs defaults,_netdev 0 0. autofs mounts on demand: install autofs, add a master map (/etc/auto.master.d/name.autofs containing /home/guests /etc/auto.guests), create the map (* -rw,sync server:/home/guests/& for wildcard homes, or user1 -rw server:/path), then systemctl enable --now autofs. Access the path to trigger the mount.

Grow online with lvextend -r -L 3G /dev/vg/lv (or +1G); without -r, run xfs_growfs /mountpoint or resize2fs /dev/vg/lv. If the VG is full, add a PV with vgextend. Aim for the middle of any allowed size range. Permission problems: check each directory on the path (x bit), ownership, group membership, SGID for shared folders, and ACLs (getfacl, setfacl -m).

tips: XFS grows online but never shrinks.
lvextend -r grows the file system in the same step.
autofs: master map + map file + enable --now autofs.
Use _netdev for network mounts in fstab.
Pick sizes in the middle of a requested range.
terms: Default RHEL file system; grow with xfs_growfs.
Linux file system that can grow and shrink.
FAT file system for USB drives and EFI partitions.
Network File System for sharing directories.
Service that mounts file systems on demand.
fstab option that waits for networking.

slides.title: File systems
script: This module covers creating file systems, mounting network shares, growing volumes, and fixing permission problems.
Each task must keep working after a reboot.

slides.title: Create and mount
script: Format with the requested type, create the mount point, and add an fstab line by UUID or label.
VFAT doesn't store Unix owners, so set uid, gid, and umask options if users need access.

slides.title: autofs for NFS homes
script: autofs mounts NFS shares only when someone accesses them. The master map names the parent directory and the map file.
A wildcard map with star and ampersand mounts each user's directory from the server automatically.

slides.title: Growing logical volumes
script: Grow a logical volume and its file system together with lvextend dash r. Plus adds to the size; without plus it sets the total.
If the volume group has no free space, add a new physical volume with vgextend first.

slides.title: Review: file systems
script: You've finished the file systems module. RHCSA is fully hands-on, so repeat each task in the labs until you can do it without looking anything up.

modules.title: Deploy, configure, and maintain systems
modules.summary: Schedule tasks with at, cron, and systemd timers; manage services at boot; set the default target; configure time synchronization; install and update software from RPM and Flatpak repositories; and modify the bootloader.

guide.html: These tasks keep a system running long term: repositories and packages, scheduled jobs, time sync, boot defaults, and kernel arguments.

Repositories: create /etc/yum.repos.d/name.repo with [id], name=, baseurl=, enabled=1, gpgcheck= (and gpgkey=), or use dnf config-manager --add-repo URL. Verify with dnf repolist. Packages: dnf install/remove/upgrade/info/search/provides, rpm -q, rpm -qf. Flatpak: flatpak remote-add --if-not-exists name URL, flatpak install name app-id, flatpak list.

cron: crontab -e -u user with min hour dom mon dow command (*/5 * * * * is every 5 minutes); verify with crontab -l -u user. One-time: echo cmd | at now + 10 minutes (atd must run). systemd timers: a .timer with OnCalendar= and Persistent=true paired with a .service; enable the timer.

Time: timedatectl set-timezone, /etc/chrony.conf server host iburst, systemctl restart chronyd, chronyc sources. Boot: systemctl set-default; services enabled at boot. Bootloader: grubby --default-kernel, grubby --set-default, grubby --update-kernel=ALL --args="..." or edit /etc/default/grub and run grub2-mkconfig -o /boot/grub2/grub.cfg.

tips: Check repos with dnf repolist before installing.
*/5 in the minute field = every 5 minutes.
Enable the .timer, not the .service.
chrony: server NAME iburst, restart chronyd, chronyc sources.
grubby changes kernel args and default kernel.
terms: Source of RPM packages defined in a .repo file.
Sandboxed desktop application packaging with remotes.
Tool for editing boot entries and kernel arguments.

slides.title: Deploy and maintain
script: This module covers keeping a system maintained: software sources, scheduled work, accurate time, and the boot configuration.
These tasks are quick points if you know the exact files and commands.

slides.title: Repositories
script: Point the system at the provided repositories by writing a repo file with an id, a name, the base URL, enabled, and the GPG settings.
Check with dnf repolist, then install packages.

slides.title: Scheduling work
script: Recurring jobs go in a user's crontab: minute, hour, day of month, month, and day of week.
Use at for one-time jobs and systemd timers when you want persistence and logging.

slides.title: Time and the bootloader
script: Set the time zone with timedatectl and sync time with chrony using a server line and a restart.
Set the default target with systemctl, and change kernel arguments or the default kernel with grubby.

slides.title: Review: deploying and maintaining systems

modules.title: Manage basic networking
modules.summary: Configure IPv4 and IPv6 addresses, gateways, and DNS with NetworkManager, set the hostname, configure name resolution, and make network services start at boot.

guide.html: You'll set static addressing persistently, configure hostname and name resolution, and verify connectivity. A mistake here can cut you off from the grader, so check your work.

List connections with nmcli con show and devices with nmcli dev status. Modify: nmcli con mod NAME ipv4.addresses 172.25.250.11/24 ipv4.gateway 172.25.250.254 ipv4.dns 172.25.250.254 ipv4.method manual connection.autoconnect yes, then nmcli con up NAME. IPv6: ipv6.addresses fd00::11/64 ipv6.method manual. Profiles are stored as keyfiles in /etc/NetworkManager/system-connections/. nmtui is a menu alternative. See man nmcli-examples.
hostnamectl set-hostname servera.lab.example.com (writes /etc/hostname). Static entries in /etc/hosts. Verify with ip addr, ip route, ping, host/dig/getent hosts, and ss -tlnp for services.

tips: Set ipv4.method manual when you add a static address.
nmcli con up NAME applies changes.
Use +ipv4.addresses to add rather than replace.
hostnamectl set-hostname is persistent.
man nmcli-examples has ready-to-adapt commands.
terms: NetworkManager's profile file format in RHEL 10.
Router for traffic leaving the local subnet.
Tool that sets the system hostname.

slides.title: Basic networking
script: This module covers network configuration with NetworkManager, which is what RHEL uses on every system.
Changes must persist, so always configure the connection profile rather than the live interface.

slides.title: Static addressing
script: Modify the connection profile with the address and prefix, gateway, and DNS server, and set the method to manual.
Then bring the connection up. Add IPv6 with the ipv6 dot properties in the same way.

slides.title: Names and checks
script: Set the hostname with hostnamectl and add static names to etc hosts if a task asks.
Verify the address, route, and name resolution before moving on.

modules.title: Manage users and groups
modules.summary: Create, delete, and modify local users and groups, set passwords and password aging, manage group membership, and configure superuser access.

guide.html: User tasks are quick but precise: exact UIDs, shells, supplementary groups, aging rules, and sudo access.

groupadd [-g GID] name; useradd -u UID -G group1,group2 -s /bin/bash name; -s /sbin/nologin for no interactive login. Set passwords non-interactively: echo 'Passw0rd' | passwd --stdin name. Modify with usermod -aG (append), -s, -L/-U; delete with userdel -r. Verify with id and getent passwd.

Per user: chage -M 30 name (max days), -m min, -W warning, -E YYYY-MM-DD expiry, -d 0 force change, -l list. Defaults for new users: PASS_MAX_DAYS etc. in /etc/login.defs. Superuser access: members of wheel have full sudo; or create /etc/sudoers.d/name with %group ALL=(ALL) ALL (add NOPASSWD: only if required) using visudo -f.

tips: -G sets supplementary groups; -g sets the primary group.
usermod -aG appends; forgetting -a removes other groups.
passwd --stdin is the quick non-interactive way on RHEL.
login.defs affects only users created afterward.
Validate sudoers drop-ins with visudo.
terms: Additional group a user belongs to.
Defaults for new accounts, such as PASS_MAX_DAYS.
Group with full sudo access on RHEL.

slides.title: Users and groups
script: This module covers local accounts, which are some of the quickest points on the exam if you're precise.
Double-check UIDs, group names, shells, and passwords after every task.

slides.title: Creating accounts
script: Create groups first, then users with the requested UID, supplementary groups, and shell.
Set the password with passwd dash dash stdin, and verify with id.

slides.title: Aging and superuser access
script: Use chage to set aging on existing users and login dot defs for the defaults that new users get.
Grant admin rights by adding users to wheel or by writing a sudoers drop-in for a group.

modules.title: Manage security
modules.summary: Configure firewalld, set default file permissions, configure key-based SSH, and manage SELinux: modes, file and process contexts, restoring contexts, port labels, and booleans.

guide.html: Security tasks often combine: for example, make Apache serve content from a nonstandard directory on a nonstandard port with SELinux enforcing and the firewall open.

firewall-cmd --get-default-zone, --list-all. Add permanently and apply: firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=http or --add-port=82/tcp, then firewall-cmd --reload. Remove with --remove-service. Rich rules restrict by source. Without --permanent changes vanish at reload or reboot.

Modes: getenforce, setenforce 0|1 (runtime), SELINUX=enforcing in /etc/selinux/config (boot). Contexts: ls -Z, ps -eZ. Persistent file labels: semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_content_t "/srv/web(/.*)?" then restorecon -Rv /srv/web; chcon is temporary. Port labels: semanage port -a -t http_port_t -p tcp 82; list with semanage port -l. Booleans: getsebool -a, setsebool -P name on. Diagnose with ausearch -m AVC -ts recent or sealert.

Key-based SSH: ssh-keygen, then ssh-copy-id user@host; keep ~/.ssh at 700 and authorized_keys at 600. Default permissions come from umask: 022 → 644/755, 027 → 640/750, 077 → 600/700; set it per user in ~/.bashrc or globally in /etc/profile.d/.

tips: firewall-cmd: --permanent then --reload.
semanage fcontext + restorecon = permanent labels; chcon = temporary.
Nonstandard web port needs semanage port and a firewall rule.
setsebool -P makes booleans survive reboots.
Never finish with SELinux permissive or disabled.
terms: firewalld trust level holding rules for interfaces and sources.
Label of user:role:type:level on files and processes.
SELinux rules based on types such as httpd_t and httpd_sys_content_t.
Resets files to their default SELinux labels.
SELinux type assigned to a network port.
On/off switch for optional SELinux policy.
Mask that removes permissions from new files.

slides.title: Managing security
script: The security module covers the controls RHEL enables by default: the firewall and SELinux, plus SSH keys and default permissions.
The exam expects SELinux to stay enforcing, so learn to fix labels instead of turning it off.

slides.title: Firewall rules
script: firewalld rules are runtime unless you add dash dash permanent. Add the service or port permanently, then reload to apply it.
List the zone to check your work.

slides.title: SELinux labels
script: Every file and process has a context. Apache, running as httpd t, can only read files labeled for web content.
Record the rule with semanage fcontext, then apply it with restorecon. chcon changes are lost on relabel.

slides.title: Ports and booleans
script: To run a service on a nonstandard port, label the port with semanage port, open the firewall, and restart the service.
Booleans switch optional policy on or off; dash capital P makes them persistent. Read denials with ausearch or sealert.

slides.title: SSH keys and umask
script: Generate a key pair and copy the public key to the other server for passwordless login.
Control default permissions for new files with umask in the user's bashrc.

script: You've finished the security module. RHCSA is fully hands-on, so repeat each task in the labs until you can do it without looking anything up.
